```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Fan chart of the accepted set of responses to a contractionary monetary policy shock identified by sign restrictions imposed on impact only. Dark band 68%, light band 90%, line the median of the accepted draws."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.9))
hor = np.arange(H_r + 1)
for row, (ax, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes, row_lab)):
    ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[0, :, row], fan_q[4, :, row], color="firebrick", alpha=0.15)
    ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[1, :, row], fan_q[3, :, row], color="firebrick", alpha=0.32)
    ax.plot(hor, fan_q[2, :, row], color="firebrick", lw=1.8)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=10)
fig.suptitle("Sign-restricted responses to a contractionary policy shock")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The restrictions bite hard. Only about one rotation in five satisfies three inequalities on
impact, so four fifths of the rotations the likelihood cannot distinguish are ruled out by
three sign statements, and extending the same restrictions over the first three months
roughly halves the acceptance rate again. By the derivation above that acceptance rate is
itself an estimate: it is the posterior probability, under a uniform prior over rotations,
that a randomly chosen structural explanation of these data is a contractionary policy shock
of this kind.

What comes out is the textbook monetary transmission that the recursive schemes failed to
deliver. The industrial production level falls, reaching a trough of $-0.690$ percent at
ten months, then recovering only partially to $-0.586$ percent by three years. The median
price level falls steadily, reaching $-0.474$ percent at three years, so the price puzzle is
gone from the median: it was an artefact of forcing the policy shock to be the funds-rate
innovation, and once we ask only for a shock that raises the rate and does not raise prices in
the impact month, the admissible rotations imply a disinflation. Honesty requires adding that
the 90 percent band on the price level at three years runs from $-0.943$ to $+0.123$ percent,
so a positive long-run price response has not been excluded, only made unlikely. The funds
rate itself rises $0.202$ percentage points on impact and then decays quickly, with the median
crossing zero as early as the seventh month, which is an implication rather than a finding: nothing was imposed beyond
the impact month, so the accepted set is free to contain rotations in which the tightening
reverses, and it does.

The bands are the point of the exercise. The 68 percent band on the output level at one year runs from
$-1.081$ to $-0.234$ percent and the 90 percent band from $-1.257$ to $-0.073$ percent, and
$97.3$ percent of the accepted draws have a negative output level at that horizon, so the
direction survives even though it was never imposed beyond impact. Those bands are wider than the recursive ones and they should be,
because they carry two kinds of uncertainty at once. Part is posterior uncertainty about $B$
and $\Sigma$, which shrinks with the sample. The rest is the spread across the admissible
rotations, which does not: even with an infinite sample, three sign restrictions on impact
would leave a set of observationally equivalent structural models, and the width of the fan
would settle at the width of that set rather than collapsing to a line.

The three identification schemes are easiest to compare with their output responses on one
axis.

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-three-schemes
#| fig-cap: "The response of the industrial production level to a contractionary policy shock under three identification schemes on identical reduced-form draws. Only the identifying assumption differs."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hor, q_last[1, :, 0], "-", color="steelblue", lw=1.8,
        label="recursive, rate ordered last")
ax.plot(hor, q_first[1, :, 0], "--", color="seagreen", lw=1.8,
        label="recursive, rate ordered first")
ax.plot(hor, fan_q[2, :, 0], "-", color="firebrick", lw=1.8,
        label="sign restrictions on impact")
ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[1, :, 0], fan_q[3, :, 0], color="firebrick", alpha=0.18)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)")
ax.set_ylabel("response of the IP level (%)")
ax.set_title("One reduced form, three identifying assumptions, three answers")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"IP level at h=12: ordered last {q_last[1, 12, 0]:.3f}, "
      f"ordered first {q_first[1, 12, 0]:.3f}, sign-restricted {fan_q[2, 12, 0]:.3f}")
print(f"IP level at h=36: ordered last {q_last[1, 36, 0]:.3f}, "
      f"ordered first {q_first[1, 36, 0]:.3f}, sign-restricted {fan_q[2, 36, 0]:.3f}")
```

Three lines, one reduced form, one data set, one posterior for $(B, \Sigma)$. At twelve
months the recursive scheme with the rate last says output is $0.120$ percent below trend,
the same scheme with the rate first says it is $0.109$ percent *above*, and the
sign-restricted median says $0.671$ percent below, more than five times the first figure. The spread
across the three lines is not sampling error and would not shrink with more data. It is the
price of the identifying assumption, and the only way to argue about it is in economic terms.

### Forecast error variance decomposition

Impulse responses answer how a variable moves after a shock. The forecast error variance
decomposition answers a different and often more policy-relevant question: of all the
uncertainty about a variable $h$ months ahead, what fraction is attributable to each
structural shock? Since the structural shocks are uncorrelated with unit variance, the
$h$-step forecast error is $\sum_{s=0}^{h}\Psi_s B_0 \varepsilon_{t+h-s}$ and its variance
decomposes additively, so the share of shock $j$ in variable $i$ is
$$
\text{FEVD}_{ij}(h) = \frac{\sum_{s=0}^{h}\left[\Psi_s B_0\right]_{ij}^2}
{\sum_{l=1}^{m}\sum_{s=0}^{h}\left[\Psi_s B_0\right]_{il}^2},
$$
the cumulated squared impulse responses of variable $i$ to shock $j$ divided by the same sum
over all shocks. We compute it under the recursive scheme with the rate ordered last, on
every fifth retained draw so the posterior bands come cheaply.

```{python}
def fevd_r(B, Sigma, order, H, m, p):
    ir = irf_r(B, chol_impact_r(Sigma, order, m), H, m, p)
    cum = np.cumsum(ir**2, axis=0)
    return cum / cum.sum(axis=2, keepdims=True)

fe = np.array([fevd_r(B_draws[i], S_draws[i], order_last, H_r, m_r, p_r)
               for i in range(0, len(B_draws), 5)])
fe_q = np.quantile(fe, [0.16, 0.5, 0.84], axis=0)
shock_lab = ["output shock", "inflation shock", "policy shock"]
for h in (0, 6, 12, 36):
    print(f"median FEVD at h = {h} (rows: variable, columns: shock)")
    print(pd.DataFrame(fe_q[1, h], index=names_r, columns=shock_lab).round(3))
print(f"\npolicy shock share of the funds rate variance at h=0, 12, 36: "
      f"{np.round(fe_q[1, [0, 12, 36], 2, 2], 3)}")
print(f"policy shock share of output variance at h=12, 36: "
      f"{np.round(fe_q[1, [12, 36], 0, 2], 3)}, "
      f"68% band at h=36 [{fe_q[0, 36, 0, 2]:.3f}, {fe_q[2, 36, 0, 2]:.3f}]")
print(f"policy shock share of inflation variance at h=12, 36: "
      f"{np.round(fe_q[1, [12, 36], 1, 2], 3)}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-fevd
#| fig-cap: "Forecast error variance decomposition of the real monthly BVAR under the recursive scheme with the funds rate ordered last. Each panel is one variable; the shares sum to one at every horizon."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
for i, (ax, nm) in enumerate(zip(axes, names_r)):
    ax.stackplot(np.arange(H_r + 1), *[fe_q[1, :, i, j] for j in range(m_r)],
                 labels=shock_lab, alpha=0.85,
                 colors=["steelblue", "seagreen", "firebrick"])
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_title(nm, fontsize=10)
    if i == 0:
        ax.set_ylabel("share of forecast error variance")
axes[2].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left")
fig.suptitle("Who moves what: variance shares by structural shock")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The decomposition delivers a result that every monetary VAR finds and that is worth stating
plainly. The policy shock explains almost all of the short-run variance of the policy rate,
$96.4$ percent on impact, which is close to a tautology given that the rate is ordered last
and therefore absorbs everything left over within the month. That share then falls steadily
to $46.5$ percent at three years, with output shocks taking over $39.9$ percent: over longer
horizons the funds rate is mostly explained by the economy the Federal Reserve is reacting
to, not by its own surprises, which is what a systematic policy rule implies.

The interesting cells are the other two rows. The policy shock accounts for $0.7$ percent of
the three-year-ahead forecast error variance of industrial production growth and $5.8$
percent of inflation's. Monetary policy surprises are, on this identification, a small part
of macroeconomic volatility. That is not a statement that monetary policy does not matter:
the systematic component of policy, the part that responds predictably to output and
inflation, is embedded in the estimated coefficients and is not a shock at all, so it
contributes nothing to this decomposition by construction. What the table says is that the
*unpredictable* part of policy is a minor driver, which is the conclusion of the empirical
monetary literature and the reason policy analysis moved towards studying rules rather than
shocks. Notice also the top-left cell at horizon zero: output growth is attributed entirely
to its own shock on impact, which is not a finding but the recursive ordering repeating itself
back to us, a reminder that every number in this table inherits the timing assumption whose
fragility the previous section demonstrated.

## Three system priors that should not share one label

The supplied readings use several computationally different VAR priors.
With fixed $\Sigma$, a Normal Minnesota coefficient prior leads to one Normal
posterior. With independent $b\sim N(b_0,V_0)$ and an inverse-Wishart prior for
$\Sigma$, the two **full conditionals** are standard, but joint direct sampling
does not follow from that fact. The Gibbs sampler alternates them.

Under a matrix-Normal inverse-Wishart prior instead,
$B\mid\Sigma\sim MN(B_0,V_0,\Sigma)$, where
$\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}B\mid\Sigma)=\Sigma\otimes V_0$.
This separable covariance buys a joint conjugate update while restricting the
relative coefficient prior covariances across equations. It remains a useful
and widely used specification; the choice is a modelling trade-off, not a
distinction between a valid and an invalid Bayesian VAR.

For identification, a draw of the reduced-form covariance still does not label
economic shocks. If $PP^\top=\Sigma$, every orthogonal rotation $PQ$ has the same
covariance because $QQ^\top=I$. Restrictions select admissible rotations; they do
not improve the reduced-form likelihood. Retain the three-variable system and
sign-restricted IRFs in the lab, and report how often proposed rotations satisfy
the restrictions. An ordering-based Cholesky illustration is not that exercise.

*Source connection:* SGPE Lecture 4, PDF pp. 3–23 and 29–35; Chan, Chapter 8;
Lopes, *Bayesian computation*, pp. 81–85, for system regression. Sign-restriction
identification follows the week's assigned specialist literature.

## Takeaways

A reduced-form VAR is heavily parameterised, so least squares overfits and the Minnesota prior earns its
place. Written as $Y = XB + U$ the model has a conjugate Normal posterior per equation given $\Sigma$,
whose mean blends the random-walk prior with the data, and simulating forward through posterior draws and
fresh shocks gives bands carrying parameter and shock uncertainty. Structural analysis is separate,
because $\Sigma$ leaves $m(m-1)/2$ rotations free: recursive identification removes them by triangularity
at the price of an ordering-dependent timing assumption, while sign restrictions keep every rotation
consistent with the assumed signs and return a set of admissible models.

On the real monthly system those abstractions acquire numbers. With $707$ observations and
$111$ coefficients the Minnesota prior compresses the total absolute lag-coefficient mass from
$8.352$ to $5.163$ without changing the reduced-form fit materially, and the resulting
posterior is the input to every identification exercise that follows. Recursive identification
then splits: ordering the funds rate last gives an impact response of output of exactly zero
and a three-year level effect of $-0.341$ percent, ordering it first gives $+0.118$ percent on
impact with non-overlapping 68 percent bands, and both orderings produce a rising price level,
the price puzzle. Three sign restrictions imposed on the impact month alone accept about one
fifth of Haar-uniform rotations, resolve the price puzzle in the median and put the output
trough at $-0.690$ percent at ten months, with $97.3$ percent of accepted draws negative at
one year even
though nothing was imposed past impact. The variance decomposition supplies the last piece of
perspective: the policy shock explains $96.4$ percent of the funds rate's own impact variance
but only $0.7$ percent of industrial production growth and $5.8$ percent of inflation at three
years, so the unpredictable part of monetary policy is a minor driver of macroeconomic
volatility even when its effects are estimated to be real.
